notes: One codebook per free-text question. Themes are multi-label; stance is single-label and coded separately, because a response can raise a theme while taking either side on it. This version merges the 2026-08-10 codebook with themes from a second inductive open-coding pass. No 2026-08-10 theme was deleted; two were split, and the mapping is recorded in retiredCodes.
[SYNTHETIC] In this public copy every theme's `examples` are synthetic stand-ins; the originals were verbatim survey answers.
sampleCaveat: Self-selected public consultation, not a probability sample. Percentages describe the people who responded, not Californians.

provenance.v2: Added from the second open-coding pass.
provenance.v3: Added from the third pass (personal question re-run).
provenance.v1_split: Derived from a 2026-08-10 code that was split into finer codes. See retiredCodes.

verification.supported: At least one verbatim quote from an identified response is attached.
verification.needs_verification: Proposed by the coding pass but returned without a citable quote. Confirm against the data before reporting any number for this code. If unsupported after review, delete it rather than leaving it at zero.
verification._why: Codes flagged here were proposed to satisfy a content quota and could not be evidenced. Audits of all three coding passes (2026-08-18) found the same root cause with three different symptoms. Where a quota was unsatisfiable the personal pass invented quotes and attached real IDs to them; the economy pass re-sliced four genuinely optimistic responses into six positive and uncertainty codes; the government pass declined to quote and wrote a placeholder instead, which is the correct behaviour. Quote accuracy was otherwise high: 37 of 38 economy quotes and all 29 government quotes were verbatim or near-verbatim. Treat a citation as a pointer to check rather than as evidence, and make quotas conditional in any re-run. This failure requires the model to generate an ID and so does not apply to the tagging pass, where IDs come from the input.

stance.question: Overall orientation toward AI expressed in this response

values.definition: Expresses concern, harm, or opposition without meaningful counterweight.
Expresses benefit, optimism, or support without meaningful counterweight.
Names both a benefit and a concern, or endorses an action while warning about it. Use this rather than forcing a side.
Descriptive or procedural with no evaluative content.

timeframe.question: Optional single-label dimension for the economy and personal questions. Coded separately so that experienced and anticipated impact are never merged into one theme count.

values.definition: Describes something that has already happened.
Expected within roughly the next few years.
Expected over a generation or longer.

retiredCodes.question: economy
retiredCodes.reason: Conflated pay effects with consumer price effects, which respondents raise separately and which imply different policy responses.
retiredCodes.migration: Re-code any response previously tagged WAGES_PRICES against both successors. A response may receive one, the other, or both.

retiredCodes.question: personal
retiredCodes.reason: Collapsed four distinct situations that differ in who made the decision: the respondent, the employer, or the nature of the work.
retiredCodes.migration: NON_USER is retained with a narrowed definition. Re-code existing NON_USER responses against all four.

questions.prompt: How do you expect AI to impact the economy?

themes.label: Job losses and displacement
themes.definition: Work disappearing, being automated away, or people being replaced.
excludes: Effects on the respondent's own job (that belongs to the personal question)
Loss of the entry route specifically (use ENTRY_PATHWAY_LOSS)

themes.label: The way in disappears
themes.definition: Concern that AI removes junior and entry-level work, so there is no longer a route into a profession or a way to build expertise.
excludes: General displacement with no career-progression claim (use JOB_LOSS)
examples: [SYNTHETIC] Worried about no way to gain experience.

themes.label: New jobs and roles
themes.definition: AI creating employment, new occupations, or new demand for skills.
excludes: Vague optimism with no employment claim

themes.label: Gains in one area, losses in another
themes.definition: Explicitly frames the effect as redistribution between sectors rather than net gain or loss.
excludes: Only one direction named (use JOB_LOSS or JOB_CREATION)

themes.label: Hits white-collar and creative work hardest
themes.definition: Claims the burden falls specifically on creative, professional, or college-educated knowledge work rather than on labour generally.
excludes: Displacement claims with no sector specified (use JOB_LOSS)
Claims framed around income class rather than occupation (use MIDDLE_CLASS_EROSION)

themes.label: Who benefits
themes.definition: Gains concentrating among owners, executives, or the wealthy while workers lose ground. Use for the general distributional claim.
excludes: Job loss with no distributional claim (use JOB_LOSS)
An explanation of the mechanism (use WEALTH_CONCENTRATION_MECHANISM)

themes.label: How the gains get captured
themes.definition: Explains the causal route by which value moves to capital owners: labour costs cut, ownership of the models, replacing wages with margin.
excludes: Stating the outcome without the route (use INEQUALITY)
examples: [SYNTHETIC] Worried about gains flow to the top.

themes.label: The middle disappears
themes.definition: Specifically claims the middle class is hollowed out, producing a polarised two-tier economy.

themes.label: Structural, not temporary
themes.definition: Claims the displacement is permanent — a population that will not be re-absorbed into work rather than a transition.
includes: shut out of work for good
excludes: Displacement described as a transition or adjustment (use JOB_LOSS)
examples: [SYNTHETIC] Worried about shut out of work for good.

themes.label: Knock-on collapse in spending
themes.definition: Reasons that unemployment feeds back into the wider economy through lost consumer spending.
examples: [SYNTHETIC] Mostly nobody has money to spend.

themes.label: Shrinking tax base and public services
themes.definition: Reasons from lost employment to lost income tax revenue to degraded public services and infrastructure.

themes.label: It's a bubble
themes.definition: Expects current AI investment to be speculative and to collapse, damaging the wider economy when it does. Note the premise: the harm comes from AI failing, not from AI working.
excludes: Harm premised on AI succeeding (use JOB_LOSS or INEQUALITY)
Reasoning specifically about business model viability (use UNPROFITABLE_MODEL)

themes.label: The businesses don't work
themes.definition: Argues AI firms have no viable path to profit and that circular investment between them is propping up the economy.
excludes: Bubble claims with no business-model reasoning (use BUBBLE_BURST)

themes.label: Cost and inefficiency
themes.definition: AI being expensive, wasteful, or adding overhead rather than saving money.
excludes: Claims about the sector's solvency (use UNPROFITABLE_MODEL)

themes.label: Efficiency and growth
themes.definition: AI raising output, speed, or economic growth.
excludes: Growth expected only under stated conditions (use CONDITIONAL_OUTCOME)

themes.label: A tool, not a replacement
themes.definition: Expects AI to extend what workers can do rather than substitute for them, with human judgement still required.
excludes: Productivity claims with no human-role argument (use PRODUCTIVITY)

themes.label: Like previous technology waves
themes.definition: Frames AI as a normal technological transition, reasoning from past waves that displaced work and then settled.
excludes: Optimism with no precedent argument (use PRODUCTIVITY)

themes.label: Depends what we do about it
themes.definition: Makes the forecast explicitly contingent on policy, regulation, adoption speed, or how well workers and institutions adapt.
includes: hinges on the pace of adoption
conditional on gains being distributed widely
excludes: Not knowing what will happen (use UNCERTAIN)
examples: [SYNTHETIC] Mostly hinges on the pace of adoption.

themes.label: Doubts the work is any good
themes.definition: Questions whether AI output is competent enough to justify its economic role.

themes.label: Downward pressure on pay
themes.definition: Pay falling or stagnating for the jobs that remain, as distinct from jobs disappearing.
examples: [SYNTHETIC] Worried about forced into lower-paying work.

themes.label: Things get more expensive
themes.definition: Rising prices for households — food, housing, energy, everyday goods — as an economic consequence of AI.
excludes: Utility bills traced specifically to data centres (use UTILITY_COSTS)

themes.label: Energy and water bills
themes.definition: Data centre demand passing through to residents as higher electricity or water rates.
excludes: Environmental damage framed as harm to a place (use LOCAL_ENVIRONMENT)
examples: [SYNTHETIC] Worried about energy prices near data centres.

themes.label: Local environmental cost
themes.definition: Water, land, power, or agricultural damage framed as an economic harm to a place, including effects on property values and local livability.
excludes: Environmental policy asks (use the government codebook)

themes.label: Environmental damage spreads through the economy
themes.definition: Chain reasoning from environmental harm outward to costs across unrelated sectors — food, manufacturing, retail, insurance.
excludes: Damage confined to the host community (use LOCAL_ENVIRONMENT)
examples: [SYNTHETIC] Mostly affects the cost of everything.

themes.label: Health as an economic factor
themes.definition: Population health effects reasoned through to economic consequences.
excludes: Health mentioned with no economic link

themes.label: California specifically
themes.definition: Frames the economic effect as particular to California — its rates, land, water, industries, or cost base — rather than general.
excludes: National or global claims with no California framing
examples: [SYNTHETIC] Worried about residents priced out of California.

themes.label: How work is valued
themes.definition: Questions how people should be compensated, or where meaning comes from, if AI does the work.
examples: [SYNTHETIC] Mostly sources of meaning in life.

themes.label: Social and political instability
themes.definition: Expects mass unemployment or inequality to produce civil unrest, or expects surveillance to be used to contain it.
excludes: Inequality with no instability claim (use INEQUALITY)

themes.label: Components and electronics cost more
themes.definition: AI build-out bidding up memory, chips, and computer parts, raising prices for consumer electronics and equipment in unrelated industries.
examples: [SYNTHETIC] We've seen electronics market distorted already.

themes.label: Firms will reverse course
themes.definition: Expects employers to abandon AI deployments and rehire people once the costs and failures land — a prediction of correction rather than permanent displacement.
excludes: Doubts about output quality alone (use QUALITY_DOUBT)
examples: [SYNTHETIC] Mostly technical debt AI can't maintain.
[SYNTHETIC] We've seen rehired at lower pay already.

themes.label: The jobs left are worse jobs
themes.definition: Expects AI to generate gig, contract, and annotation work with lower pay and no protections, replacing salaried employment rather than eliminating work outright.
excludes: Net new employment framed positively (use JOB_CREATION)
Pay falling in existing roles (use WAGE_SUPPRESSION)

themes.label: The public doesn't want it
themes.definition: Expects negative public sentiment toward AI output to limit adoption or damage the businesses that rely on it.
examples: [SYNTHETIC] Mostly public distaste for AI output.
[SYNTHETIC] Worried about readers wary of AI-flooded markets.

themes.label: Facilities don't deliver the jobs promised
themes.definition: Disputes the economic development case for data centres — few permanent jobs relative to the land, power, and public cost consumed.
excludes: Environmental harm to the area (use LOCAL_ENVIRONMENT)
examples: [SYNTHETIC] Worried about no lasting job security.

themes.label: Fewer people will pursue education
themes.definition: Expects the collapse of graduate career paths to reduce enrolment in higher education, with knock-on effects on the skill base and civic life.
examples: [SYNTHETIC] Mostly degrees no longer worth it.
[SYNTHETIC] Worried about graduates pushed into manual jobs.
[SYNTHETIC] We've seen weakened civic engagement already.

themes.label: Doesn't know or won't predict
themes.definition: Declines to forecast, or says the outcome is unknowable.
excludes: Blank or non-answers, which are excluded before coding
A forecast conditioned on a named factor (use CONDITIONAL_OUTCOME)

questions.prompt: What do you think the government should do about these impacts?

themes.label: Regulate, unspecified
themes.definition: Calls for regulation, rules, or oversight without naming a specific mechanism.
excludes: A named mechanism such as tax or disclosure (code that instead)

themes.label: Limit, curb, or ban
themes.definition: Calls to stop, reverse, or forbid AI use in some or all domains.
excludes: Regulation that permits continued use (use REGULATE)

themes.label: Pause and study first
themes.definition: Asks for deployment to slow or stop temporarily while impacts are assessed, rather than for a permanent prohibition.

themes.label: Corporate disclosure
themes.definition: Requiring companies to publish information they currently withhold about their operations, training, ownership, or impacts.

themes.label: Label AI-generated output
themes.definition: Requiring AI-produced content or AI involvement to be marked so people can tell and can choose.
examples: [SYNTHETIC] Worried about visible AI labels on goods.

themes.label: Environmental and energy impact
themes.definition: Water, power, emissions, or footprint given as the reason for action.
excludes: The specific instrument of siting control (use DATA_CENTER_LIMITS)

themes.label: Control where facilities are built
themes.definition: Siting, permitting, land-use, or construction controls on AI infrastructure — the instrument, whatever the stated rationale.
excludes: Environmental concern with no facility-level ask (use ENVIRONMENT)

themes.label: Tax and financial levers
themes.definition: Taxes, levies, subsidies, or funding conditions aimed at AI companies.
excludes: Taxation with a stated destination for the revenue (also code REDISTRIBUTION or UBI)

themes.label: Universal basic income
themes.definition: Names basic income, a living wage stipend, or an equivalent unconditional payment as the response to displacement.

themes.label: Share the gains
themes.definition: Proposals to spread AI-generated wealth through social programs, public services, or shared ownership.
includes: AI tax revenue for safety nets
excludes: Taxation with no stated use of the revenue (use TAXATION)
examples: [SYNTHETIC] Mostly AI tax revenue for safety nets.

themes.label: Retraining and transition funding
themes.definition: Publicly funded or employer-funded reskilling, continuing education, and workforce transition support.

themes.label: Protect workers
themes.definition: General job security, displacement support, or limits on replacing workers.
excludes: An outright prohibition on AI replacing people (use REPLACEMENT_BAN)

themes.label: Make AI replacement of workers illegal
themes.definition: Asks for a legal prohibition on eliminating, demoting, or reducing the pay of a human because of AI, rather than for mitigation of it.
includes: favoring people over automation in hiring
no loss of income to AI
examples: [SYNTHETIC] Worried about favoring people over automation in hiring.

themes.label: Conditions on AI-driven layoffs
themes.definition: Procedural requirements when roles are cut for AI — notice periods, reporting, WARN-style rules.

themes.label: Collective bargaining
themes.definition: Strengthening unions or bargaining rights as the route to controlling AI in the workplace.
examples: [SYNTHETIC] Mostly protect union and non-union labourers.

themes.label: Legal accountability for harms
themes.definition: Making companies legally answerable for damage their AI systems cause or for the consequences of deploying them.

themes.label: Consent and payment for training data
themes.definition: Requiring permission, credit, or compensation for work used to train models, and enforcing copyright against developers.
examples: [SYNTHETIC] Worried about opt out of training.

themes.label: Protect creative professions
themes.definition: Action aimed at the livelihoods of artists, writers, photographers, musicians, and other creative workers.

themes.label: Privacy and surveillance limits
themes.definition: Restricting AI-enabled monitoring, data collection, or use of personal information — including of employees.
includes: look to countries with stronger privacy law

themes.label: Safety oversight
themes.definition: Oversight framed specifically around safety or harm prevention.

themes.label: Rules for government's own use of AI
themes.definition: How public agencies should adopt, restrict, or govern AI in their own operations — including procurement, data handling, and human oversight of automated decisions.
includes: run models locally on government data
don't deploy untested software in public services
excludes: Rules aimed at private companies (code those instead)
examples: [SYNTHETIC] Mostly run models locally on government data.
[SYNTHETIC] Worried about human review of AI decisions.
[SYNTHETIC] We've seen don't deploy untested software in public services already.

themes.label: Schools and education policy
themes.definition: Action aimed at how AI is used in teaching, learning, or academic integrity.

themes.label: Names acceptable uses
themes.definition: Carves out domains where AI should be allowed or encouraged, usually alongside restrictions elsewhere.
excludes: Unqualified support for AI (that is stance, not a theme)

themes.label: Let the affected public decide
themes.definition: Requires direct community or voter approval for AI infrastructure and policy, rather than decisions by officials alone.
includes: voter consent for data centre siting
examples: [SYNTHETIC] Mostly voter consent for data centre siting.

themes.label: Legislate with people who understand it
themes.definition: Argues rules must be drafted in consultation with technical subject-matter experts, usually citing past legislation that was unworkable.
includes: policymakers out of their depth on tech
excludes: Doubt about government capability with no remedy (use GOV_INCOMPETENCE)

themes.label: Look to other jurisdictions or history
themes.definition: Points to other countries, states, or historical precedent as a model.

themes.label: Government can't do this well
themes.definition: Doubts the state's technical or institutional capacity to regulate AI, citing a poor track record. Distinct from opposing intervention in principle.

themes.label: Industry will control the process
themes.definition: Expects any regulation to be shaped or neutralised by the companies it targets, or doubts anything will be enforced.
examples: [SYNTHETIC] Mostly policy bent toward corporate power.
[SYNTHETIC] Worried about rules need enforcement to matter.

themes.label: Warns against overreach or censorship
themes.definition: Cautions that government action could suppress speech, stifle innovation, or go too far. Code this even when it appears alongside a call for regulation.
excludes: Straightforward opposition to all action (use NO_ACTION)

themes.label: Let people turn it off
themes.definition: A right to decline AI — opt-in defaults, a working off switch, and no penalty in price or service for refusing.
includes: protect workers who decline to use it
examples: [SYNTHETIC] We've seen protect workers who decline to use it already.

themes.label: A human has to decide
themes.definition: Requires a person to make or review consequential decisions — employment, healthcare, benefits, safety-critical and military systems — with AI confined to an advisory role.
includes: humans must decide in high-stakes sectors
excludes: Prohibiting AI replacement of workers (use REPLACEMENT_BAN)
examples: [SYNTHETIC] Worried about mandate humans in named occupations.
[SYNTHETIC] We've seen humans must decide in high-stakes sectors already.

themes.label: Restrict AI in recruitment
themes.definition: Rules aimed specifically at automated screening and hiring — prohibition, bias testing, or disclosure that AI was used.
includes: openness on AI in personnel choices
excludes: Human review of decisions generally (use HUMAN_DECISION)
examples: [SYNTHETIC] Mostly keep AI out of hiring.
[SYNTHETIC] Worried about bias testing for hiring tools.
[SYNTHETIC] We've seen openness on AI in personnel choices already.

themes.label: Data centres pay their own way
themes.definition: Requires AI infrastructure to bear its own utility and grid costs rather than passing them to residents, including rate freezes and separate accounting.
includes: don't drive up bills for residents
examples: [SYNTHETIC] Mostly cover grid upgrade costs themselves.
[SYNTHETIC] Worried about cap household utility rates.
[SYNTHETIC] We've seen don't drive up bills for residents already.

themes.label: AI output shouldn't be copyrightable
themes.definition: Denies copyright protection to AI-generated material, as distinct from protecting the work used to train the model.
excludes: Consent and payment for training data (use IP_CONSENT)
examples: [SYNTHETIC] Mostly prompt writers get no copyright.
[SYNTHETIC] Worried about GenAI works never registrable.

themes.label: Criminalise specific misuses
themes.definition: Targets named malicious applications — deepfakes, impersonation, fraud, malware, non-consensual imagery — rather than AI development generally.
examples: [SYNTHETIC] Worried about fake evidence and insurance fraud.

themes.label: Protect people the systems interact with
themes.definition: Accountability for psychological and medical harm to people using AI directly — chatbots substituting for care, reinforcing delusion, or giving dangerous advice.
excludes: Errors affecting the respondent's work (use the personal codebook)
examples: [SYNTHETIC] Mostly AI as mental health substitute.
[SYNTHETIC] We've seen harmful advice to vulnerable users already.

themes.label: Government should stay out
themes.definition: Opposes intervention, or argues the market or existing law is sufficient.
excludes: Support for action with a caveat (use SPEECH_CAUTION alongside the action)
Wanting action but doubting competence (use GOV_INCOMPETENCE)

questions.prompt: How has AI impacted your job and workplace, if at all?

themes.label: Required to use it
themes.definition: The employer requires, pressures, or pushes AI use regardless of whether it helps. The defining feature is that the decision came from above.
excludes: AI appearing in software without anyone choosing it (use TOOL_IMPOSED)
examples: [SYNTHETIC] Mostly forced to use it daily.
[SYNTHETIC] We've seen administrators pushing Copilot already.

themes.label: It showed up in the software
themes.definition: AI features added to existing tools by vendors without the organisation or user asking for them, and often without a way to opt out.
includes: prompts added to every email draft
examples: [SYNTHETIC] Mostly prompts added to every email draft.
[SYNTHETIC] Worried about AI built into all software.
[SYNTHETIC] We've seen imposed on clients unasked already.

themes.label: Deployed without preparation
themes.definition: Tools introduced with inadequate training, guidance, or thought about purpose, so staff absorb the cost of figuring it out.
excludes: The requirement to use it (use MANDATED_USE)
examples: [SYNTHETIC] Worried about adopted without clear purpose.

themes.label: More work, not less
themes.definition: AI increasing the respondent's workload rather than reducing it.

themes.label: Checking the machine's work
themes.definition: A new role or workflow built around verifying, correcting, or cleaning up AI output the respondent's own workflow produced.
excludes: Cleaning up after colleagues' AI use (use COWORKER_AI)

themes.label: Absorbing colleagues' AI use
themes.definition: Other people's use of AI creating work or problems for the respondent.
excludes: The respondent's own AI output (use VALIDATION_WORK)
examples: [SYNTHETIC] Mostly cleaning up colleagues' AI output.

themes.label: Was given wrong information
themes.definition: AI producing errors that affected the respondent's work or decisions.
excludes: Doubts about quality in the abstract (use the economy codebook)

themes.label: Communication broke down
themes.definition: AI degrading communication between people or teams.

themes.label: Loss of the human element
themes.definition: Work or interaction feeling less human, more mechanical, or less meaningful.
examples: [SYNTHETIC] Worried about losing the human touch.

themes.label: Monitored by AI at work
themes.definition: Employer AI systems monitoring the respondent, or their work artefacts being harvested to train models.
includes: emails and messages used to train AI
excludes: Privacy policy asks (use the government codebook)
examples: [SYNTHETIC] Mostly emails and messages used to train AI.
[SYNTHETIC] We've seen emails and messages used to train AI already.

themes.label: Training the thing that replaces you
themes.definition: Being asked to build, train, or improve an AI system the respondent believes will eliminate their own or colleagues' jobs.
includes: training a model that will replace me
job listings only for AI trainers
examples: [SYNTHETIC] Mostly training a model that will replace me.
[SYNTHETIC] Worried about job listings only for AI trainers.

themes.label: Already lost work
themes.definition: The respondent's role has actually been eliminated, or they have already lost income. Past tense, not anticipated.

themes.label: Own job feels at risk
themes.definition: Anticipated risk to the respondent's own role, not yet realised.
excludes: Loss that has already happened (use JOB_LOST)
examples: [SYNTHETIC] Worried about expect to be replaced.

themes.label: Lost clients or commissions
themes.definition: Self-employed, freelance, or contract workers losing custom to AI-generated substitutes.

themes.label: The field, not just the job
themes.definition: Hiring across the respondent's whole occupation drying up — freezes, ghost listings, peers out of work — whether or not the respondent personally lost a role.
excludes: The respondent's own role ending (use JOB_LOST)
examples: [SYNTHETIC] We've seen peers out of work already.

themes.label: No way in for new people
themes.definition: Junior roles and internships disappearing, so newcomers cannot get the experience the field requires.
includes: internships no longer lead to jobs
nobody knows how new people will train
examples: [SYNTHETIC] Mostly internships no longer lead to jobs.
[SYNTHETIC] We've seen nobody knows how new people will train already.

themes.label: Leaving the field
themes.definition: Changing occupation, or actively planning to, because of AI.
excludes: Job loss with no stated change of direction (use JOB_LOST)

themes.label: Pressure to work faster
themes.definition: Expectations rising because AI is assumed to make the work quicker.
excludes: More tasks without a speed framing (use ADDED_WORKLOAD)

themes.label: Own work used without consent
themes.definition: The respondent's own creative or professional output scraped, trained on, or imitated without permission or payment.
includes: a model trained on my style
excludes: Concern for creative work in general (use CREATIVITY_LOSS)
examples: [SYNTHETIC] Worried about a model trained on my style.

themes.label: Threat to creative work
themes.definition: AI displacing or devaluing art, writing, or creative practice as a category.
excludes: The respondent's own work being scraped (use IP_TAKEN)

themes.label: Damage to the profession's standing
themes.definition: AI eroding public trust in, or the quality standards of, the respondent's profession.
examples: [SYNTHETIC] Worried about professionals filing AI-written work.

themes.label: Harm to students' learning
themes.definition: Students over-relying on AI, undermining learning, retention, or critical thinking.
excludes: Policy asks about schools (use the government codebook)

themes.label: Teaching and assessment upended
themes.definition: Educators struggling to design assignments, assess honestly, or teach evaluation skills in AI's presence.

themes.label: Colleagues losing the ability
themes.definition: Adults around the respondent losing the capacity to do work, think, or generate ideas without AI.
excludes: The respondent's own skill loss (also code here, noting it)
examples: [SYNTHETIC] Mostly dependence on AI for reasoning.
[SYNTHETIC] Worried about nobody has their own ideas.
[SYNTHETIC] We've seen dependence on AI for reasoning already.

themes.label: Found it useful
themes.definition: AI helping the respondent with a concrete task, in their own account.
excludes: Usefulness reported alongside a net-negative verdict (code both)

themes.label: Chooses not to use it
themes.definition: AI is available but the respondent declines to use it, usually on ethical, professional, or risk grounds. The decision is theirs.
includes: disallowed it at our own workplace
excludes: Not being relevant to the work (use NOT_APPLICABLE)
examples: [SYNTHETIC] Worried about won't use the platform introduced.
[SYNTHETIC] We've seen disallowed it at our own workplace already.

themes.label: Doesn't use it
themes.definition: Reports not using AI personally, with no stated reason, whether or not others around them do.
excludes: A stated decision to refuse (use REFUSAL)
Uses it and finds no effect (use NO_IMPACT)

themes.label: Employer hasn't taken it up
themes.definition: The organisation has not introduced AI tools, so the question of personal use has not arisen.
themes.reviewNote: Three passes, no support. Of 44 audited responses none reported an employer that had not adopted AI. Recommend deletion unless a targeted search finds cases; a code that is genuinely at or near zero should be reported as an absence in prose, not carried as a theme.

themes.label: Doesn't apply to this kind of work
themes.definition: The nature of the work — relational, hands-on, physical, or requiring human presence — puts it outside AI's reach in the respondent's view.
examples: [SYNTHETIC] Mostly my job can't be automated.

themes.label: Little or no personal effect
themes.definition: Explicitly reports that AI has not meaningfully touched their work or life.
excludes: Blank or non-answers, which are excluded before coding
No effect on their own work but damage to their field (code FIELD_COLLAPSE as well or instead)
examples: [SYNTHETIC] Mostly no effect on own work.
[SYNTHETIC] Worried about so far, not much.

themes.label: Present but trivial
themes.definition: AI is noticeable but registers only as a low-level irritation rather than a change to the work.
excludes: Substantive workload or quality effects (code those)
examples: [SYNTHETIC] Worried about slows down the computer.

themes.label: The product itself got worse
themes.definition: The end result of the work is worse than before AI, as a standing condition rather than a discrete error to be caught.
excludes: The labour of catching errors (use VALIDATION_WORK)

themes.label: Same job, different work
themes.definition: The role persists but its content changes — often from producing to reviewing, or from craft to oversight. Distinct from losing the job or from simply having more of it.
includes: shifted from creating to reviewing AI output
examples: [SYNTHETIC] Mostly shifted from creating to reviewing AI output.
[SYNTHETIC] Worried about craft turned into mass production.

themes.label: Searching in a flooded market
themes.definition: The experience of job-hunting against a field crowded with displaced applicants and thinned postings. Note that a large share of respondents are not currently working.
excludes: The field having no openings, described from inside a job (use FIELD_COLLAPSE)

themes.label: The work stopped feeling worth doing
themes.definition: Loss of pride, dignity, or interest in the work itself because AI performs the part the respondent valued, or because effort is no longer legible to others.
includes: reading writing nobody bothered to write
excludes: Threat to creative practice as a category (use CREATIVITY_LOSS)
examples: [SYNTHETIC] Mostly lost enjoyment of the craft.
[SYNTHETIC] Worried about erodes the dignity of labor.
[SYNTHETIC] We've seen reading writing nobody bothered to write already.

themes.label: Morale and team dynamics
